summary: This 1990 Climatic Change article by Gordon J. MacDonald of The MITRE Corporation examines where methane clathrates (hydrates) are stable in permafrost and ocean sediments and how they may have affected atmospheric composition during the ice ages. It estimates the carbon stored as clathrates, argues the methane is mainly produced by anaerobic bacteria, and describes how surface changes such as flooding, sea-level drop and ice-cap growth destabilize or stabilize clathrates. The paper concludes clathrates may have produced feedbacks that amplified orbitally driven climate change.
one_line: A 1990 Climatic Change paper by Gordon J. MacDonald on methane clathrate stability and their possible role in ice-age atmospheric and climate changes.
key_facts: Methane clathrates are stable at depths greater than about 200 m in permafrost regions.
In ocean sediments, methane clathrates are stable at water depths greater than about 250 m, provided bottom waters are sufficiently cold.
Average clathrate stability zone thickness is about 400 m in cold regions with average surface temperatures below freezing.
The clathrate stability zone is about 500 m thick in ocean sediments and up to 1,500 m in regions of surface temperature below -15 °C or in the deep ocean.
The estimate of carbon stored as clathrates is about 11,000 Gt for ocean sediments and about 400 Gt for sediments under permafrost regions.
MacDonald's estimate is in rough accord with an independent estimate by Kvenvolden of 10,000 Gt.
Methane in clathrates is produced chiefly by anaerobic bacteria, according to its geologic setting, isotopic composition, and methane to ethane plus propane ratio.
Warming by ocean flooding of exposed continental shelf and pressure changes from sea-level drop destabilize clathrates under the ocean.
Ice-cap growth stabilizes clathrates under the ice cap.
The time scale for thermal destabilization of clathrates is on the order of thousands of years.
Fixing methane in clathrates after surface cooling requires several tens of thousands of years.
The release of methane and its subsequent oxidation to carbon dioxide may be responsible for observed swings in atmospheric methane and carbon dioxide during glacial times.
Methane and carbon dioxide are strong infrared absorbers, so clathrate release and trapping contribute strong feedback to radiative forcing from earth's orbital variations.
The article was published in June 1990 in volume 16, pages 247–281 of Climatic Change.
Gordon J. MacDonald was Vice President and Chief Scientist of The MITRE Corporation in McLean, VA.
